LAREDO — Alfonso "Poncho" Casso has built his run for mayor on a single sentence: nobody owns him. Speaking to Laredo's mechanical and electrical contractors on October 20, he described himself as the least-funded candidate in the race, said he refuses big money, and alleged that his rivals are "bought and paid for by either the banks or development companies." That is a testable claim — because Texas law makes every candidate show the money. Casso's 30th-day-before-election campaign finance report was filed with the City Secretary and is posted on the City of Laredo's campaign finance reports page under the October 5, 2026 deadline. It covers July 1 through September 24, 2026. It is a public record, and it is where his pitch meets the paperwork.

What the cover sheet says

The report — filled out by hand, with Casso serving as his own campaign treasurer — shows total political contributions of $4,000 for the period, total political expenditures of just $721.23, and total political contributions maintained of $3,278.77 — the cash his campaign still held on September 24. The loans section is empty: no loans taken, and an outstanding loan balance of $0. One detail of the document deserves a factual note and nothing more: the City Secretary's stamp on the report reads "REC'D OCT 7 '26, 9:06 AM" — two days after the October 5 deadline that governed this reporting period. Whether a filing met its deadline is a question for the City Secretary and the Texas Ethics Commission; Webb Watch reports the stamp on the document, and alleges nothing about it.

Whose names are on it

Schedule A1, the contribution list, holds exactly two entries. On September 4, 2026, Juan Pasquel of 4109 Nafta Blvd., Laredo, gave $3,000. On August 26, 2026, a donor at 7110 Rocio Dr., Ste. 7, Laredo, gave $1,000; the name is written in cursive and is best read as "Tebe Santos" — the first name may read "Tere," and Webb Watch flags that uncertainty rather than guess at a person's name. That is the entire list. There are no political action committee contributions and no in-kind contributions. One gap is worth noting, as a matter of completeness and not of wrongdoing: the occupation and employer fields on Schedule A1 are blank for both donors — the form asks for that information, and the filing leaves it empty. None of this is illegal either way: Texas sets no contribution limits in local races, and disclosure is exactly what the law asks. The question Casso himself put to voters is narrower — whether the names on his filing match the independence he advertises. On this filing, they do.

The money from the candidate himself

For a candidate who says nobody owns him, the most important lines in the report are his own — and in Casso's report, those lines are empty too. The filing shows no loans from the candidate (no loans from anyone) and no personal-funds spending by the candidate. His campaign is not carried by his own money, and it is not carried by the banks and development companies he criticizes: it is carried by $4,000 from two other people, and nothing else. Set beside the rest of the field, his "least-funded" description holds up. In the same period, Alyssa Cigarroa reported $374,500 in contributions; Mayor Victor Treviño's campaign runs on a $200,000 loan from the mayor himself, plus $32,122.16 in donated billboards; and JD Gonzalez lent his own campaign $104,100. Casso's campaign reported four thousand dollars in total support — the smallest pile of money in the race.

The rest of the field, for the record

Casso did file — that much is established, and it separates him from at least one rival. Under the same October 5 deadline, the City Secretary's page carries 30th-day reports for Mayor Victor D. Treviño, JD Gonzalez, Alyssa Cigarroa, and Casso. One mayoral name on the ballot, Jorge A. Garza, appears in the same list with no report linked — as of October 23, no 30th-day filing for Garza is posted. Now that every filed report in the race has been read side by side, the comparison Casso invites voters to make is settled: of the candidates who filed, his campaign is running on the least money. The final pre-election look comes with the 8th-day report, due October 26 and covering September 25 through October 24 — the stretch when early voting is already underway.

The bottom line

A campaign finance report is not an accusation. It is a list of names and numbers that the law makes public precisely so voters can weigh them. Casso has asked Laredo to judge his opponents by who funds them. His own report — a public record posted by the City Secretary — invites exactly the same judgment of him, and on the numbers in his filing, his central claim survives the test he set for everyone else: two donors, $4,000 raised, $721.23 spent, no loans, and no one's IOU in his pocket. Whether a shoestring campaign means independence is a judgment the report leaves, properly, to the voters of Laredo.

Sources: City of Laredo, Campaign Finance Reports (City Secretary's Office) — https://www.cityoflaredo.com/departments/city-secretary-s-office/campaign-finance-reports ; Alfonso "Poncho" Casso, Campaign Finance Report, 30th day before the November 3, 2026 election (posted October 8, 2026) — https://www.cityoflaredo.com/home/showpublisheddocument/24759/639270631492770000 ; Webb Watch 956, "'Nobody owns me': Poncho Casso tells Laredo contractors City Hall is 'anti business' in 10-minute campaign speech," October 21, 2026 — https://webbwatch956.com/story.html?slug=poncho-casso-contractors-speech-oct21

excerpt: Mayoral candidate Alfonso "Poncho" Casso campaigns as the least-funded man in the race who answers to no donor. His 30th-day campaign finance report — a public record filed with the City Secretary — is where that claim can actually be checked. Webb Watch 956 went to the filing, and the filing backs the pitch: $4,000 from exactly two donors, $721.23 spent, and no loans at all.
title: Follow the Money: Poncho Casso Says "Nobody Owns Me" — His Own Filing Is the Test
